The previous chapters showed how the laws of conservation of mass and conserva- tion of atomic identity, together with the concept of the mole, determine quantita- tive mass relationships in chemical reactions. That discussion assumed prior knowl- edge of the chemical formulas of the reactants and products in each equation. The far more open-ended questions of which compounds are found in nature (or which can be made in the laboratory) and what types of reactions they undergo now arise. Why are some elements and compounds violently reactive and others inert? Why are there compounds with chemical formulas H2O and NaCl, but never H3O or NaCl2? Why are helium and the other noble gases monatomic, but molecules of hydrogen and chlorine diatomic? All of these questions can be answered by exam- ining the formation of chemical bonds between atoms.
